papers.title: Why We Created Yet Another Memory Framework: Understanding MGA's Role in Next-Gen Database Systems
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带生产环境信号，关注延迟，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Despite the presence of multiple memory regions in modern database systems, supporting an efficient form of memory remains a challenge under production constraints. In enterprise-grade data systems, existing abstractions impose a trade-off between coarsegrained global sharing and strict process isolation, resulting in data copying, memory fragmentation, and limited support for controlled sharing. These challenges become more pronounced as workloads grow more diverse, and systems must tolerate process failures while maintaining predictable performance. This paper introduces the Managed Global Area (MGA), a scoped shared-memory abstraction in Oracle AI Database that addresses these limitations. MGA allows components to explicitly define allocation source, membership, and coordination semantics across selected processes while integrating with a production database engine. Unlike fully shared memory regions in Oracle, such as the System Global Area (SGA), MGA supports dynamic process membership and modular memory usage without imposing system-wide visibility. We evaluate MGA on analytical and AI workloads that stress shared-memory execution, including TPC-H hash joins and ONNX Runtime inference. Under concurrent execution, MGA reduces latency for join-intensive TPC-H queries by up to 35%. For ONNX-based inference, MGA-enabled model sharing reduces memory footprint by up to 90% and lowers large-model inference latency by up to 37%. These results demonstrate that dynamically scoped shared memory can improve both efficiency and predictability in production database systems.

papers.title: OceanBase Bacchus: A High-Performance and Scalable Cloud-Native Shared Storage Architecture for Multi-Cloud
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带生产环境信号，涉及解耦式架构
papers.abstract: Although more databases embrace shared-storage architectures, current storage-disaggregated systems lack an optimal balance between cost and performance. B+-tree-based shared storage struggles with frequent in-place updates under high concurrency; disaggregated designs still require a scalable shared-log path for multi-writer OLTP. This paper presents OceanBase Bacchus, a production-grade disaggregated shared-storage architecture for OceanBase. We foreground two technical elements: (i) service-oriented PALF logging with sharded log streams and multiple Read-Write (RW) leaders, where partition-local ordering is composed with distributed 2PC across stream leaders , breaking the single-writer bottleneck of classic shared-log designs while preserving ACID, and (ii) a Shared Block Cache Service that pools macro-blocks within an availability zone, a less common alternative to purely per-node caches and motivated by stateless compute scaling. Cloud object storage backs the LSM-tree capacity tier for cost, but we do not treat "LSM + object storage" as the headline novelty (precedents exist). Bacchus's value is integrating and hardening these mechanisms in a shipping system, demonstrated by credible OLTP/OLAP performance and substantial storage-cost reductions. The architecture decouples modules and enables elastic scaling of compute, cache, and storage independently. Experimental results show that Ocean-Base Bacchus matches or exceeds HBase and PolarDB in OLTP and significantly outperforms StarRocks in OLAP. With multi-cloud support, the system retains high availability and competitive performance while cutting storage costs by 59% (OLTP) and 89% (OLAP).

papers.title: One Ring to Shuffle Them All: Scalable Intra-Process Data Redistribution with Ring-Buffer Shuffle in Redpanda Oxla

papers.abstract: As server CPUs scale to dozens and now hundreds of cores per socket, parallel query engines must rethink how they redistribute data between threads. Partitioned operators such as hash joins and aggregations require frequent data redistribution across threads, yet existing intra-process shuffle designs fundamentally fail to scale with core count: batch partitioning avoids cross-thread synchronization in the hot path but materializes all intermediate data, introduces a global producer/consumer barrier, and requires a consumption approach with low cache locality, while channel-based streaming avoids materialization but incurs per-channel synchronization that scales poorly with core count. As core counts rise, these architectural tradeoffs increasingly prevent engines from fully utilizing modern hardware. We present a ring-buffer streaming shuffle design that addresses these shortcomings through lock-free atomic slot acquisition into fixed-size batch groups, achieving amortized O (1) synchronization cost per batch and O ( M ) memory independent of input size. Ring-buffer shuffle has been implemented in Redpanda's Oxla query engine for two years, where it currently powers production queries for Redpanda SQL users. We evaluate all three approaches on a 72-core NVIDIA Grace-Hopper, a 192-core dual-socket AWS Graviton4, and a 96-core (192-thread) AMD EPYC. On a 72-core single-socket system the ring buffer outperforms channel streaming by up to 44% and batch partitioning by up to 79%; at 192 cores the advantage over channel grows to over 100% and over 300% versus batch partitioning. Even so, on chiplet architectures with many partitioned L3 caches, the shared atomic counter becomes a cross-die bottleneck and channel-based streaming remains competitive. End-to-end Graviton4 evaluation on TPC-H (21 queries) and ClickBench (43 queries) shows the advantage is workload-shape-dependent: the ring buffer wins TPC-H in aggregate (1.07×) across diverse query shapes, but a handful of consumer-heavy patterns—COUNT(DISTINCT), wide aggregates—favor channels and swing ClickBench's aggregate the other way.

To break this impasse, we propose ScaleSense, a proactive, query-level resource scaling framework. Specifically, it features a multi-faceted query encoder that jointly models plan topologies and hardware specifications. Crucially, a quantile-based resource predictor estimates multi-dimensional physical footprints, acting as a reliable safety net for optimal resource scaling. An auto-scaling controller then navigates the performance-cost Pareto frontier, dynamically tailoring allocations to specific business priorities without requiring model retraining. Evaluations on over 1.36 million production queries show that ScaleSense achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy with good prediction interval coverage. papers.title: E-LQO: A Comprehensive Energy Evaluation Framework for Learned Query Optimization
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带基准测试，有实验评估，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Learned Query Optimization (LQO) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving database performance, with reported speedups of 2× to over 10× on standard benchmarks. Existing evaluations, however, remain largely latency-centric and leave the energy debt from data collection, model training, and online inference less visible. This paper presents E-LQO, the first comprehensive framework for evaluating energy consumption across the complete LQO lifecycle: data collection or preparation, model training, model inference, and plan execution. We formalize two domain-specific metrics— Energy Return on Investment (EROI) and Energy Payback Time (EPT)—to quantify both per-cycle efficiency and the amortization horizon of learned optimizers. Across seven LQO methods on fixed-scale JOB and on TPC-H/TPC-DS up to 100 GB, we find that lifecycle energy is governed less by whether an optimizer is learned than by how it obtains supervision. Execution-based systems buy plan quality through active exploration and carry a large upfront energy debt; passive/log-driven systems can repay much faster with reusable logs or labels, but this advantage depends on incremental-cost accounting and often comes with weaker latency gains on light workloads. We further show that total online inference energy, including candidate-plan generation, enables symmetric accounting, and that roughly 50% template coverage is the energy-optimal exploration region for the execution-based methods we study. E-LQO provides practitioners with actionable guidance for energy-conscious deployment decisions and exposes optimization opportunities for sustainable learned query optimization.

papers.abstract: Modern cloud platforms provide diverse compute services, including virtual machines, Function-as-a-Service, and Query-as-a-Service, each offering unique trade-offs in performance, elasticity, and cost. While these services collectively cover the diverse needs of OLAP workloads, existing systems typically rely on a single service type or static rule-based scheduling. However, no single service is optimal for dynamic OLAP workloads with diverse performance characteristics and resource requirements. Consequently, efficient query execution requires scheduling workloads across heterogeneous services, which introduces three challenges. (1) Heterogeneous service models. Distinct billing models and execution paradigms (e.g., stateful or stateless) complicate the comparison of services. (2) Scheduling complexity at scale. High query concurrency exacerbates resource contention, creating a vast search space that makes identifying optimal scheduling decisions in real time computationally expensive. (3) Unpredictable runtime dynamics. Cloud infrastructure exhibits performance fluctuations due to factors like multi-tenant interference and scaling delays, which can invalidate initial scheduling decisions and cause suboptimal performance. In this paper, we present EASE, a resource-aware query scheduling framework designed to orchestrate OLAP queries across heterogeneous cloud compute services. EASE addresses these challenges through three integrated mechanisms. First, EASE incorporates a heterogeneity-aware cost model that captures distinct service characteristics to guide service selection. Second, EASE employs a real-time query scheduler that resolves resource contention under high concurrency. Third, EASE implements a dynamic rescheduler that mitigates runtime fluctuations by proactively migrating queries subject to unexpected delays. Our evaluation demonstrates that EASE significantly improves query performance and cost efficiency, reducing query latency by up to 35% and monetary cost by up to 67% compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

We study HNSW hyperparameter tuning from a systems perspective and show that its configuration space exhibits strong structural regularities. Specifically, we identify monotonic, dominant unimodal, and separable relationships among search-time and construction-time parameters, which induce feasibility boundaries under performance and resource constraints. Unlike generic black-box optimizers, CHAT exploits HNSW-specific structure to perform deterministic, sample-efficient search and prune resource-infeasible configurations before full index construction. Across multiple datasets and HNSW-based vector search engines, CHAT identifies configurations that maximize recall or throughput while satisfying constraints on accuracy, latency, build time, index size, and tuning budget. Compared to strong baselines, CHAT achieves up to 45% higher throughput or 11% higher recall, and converges up to 44× faster. papers.abstract: Traditional query processing engines require continuous development and extensions to support new techniques and user requirements, and in some cases, entirely new systems must be built from scratch. An early prototype of GenDB uses LLM agents to generate instance-optimized query execution code tailored to specific data, workloads, and hardware resources. This prototype suits offline code generation for repetitive, templated queries, since the upfront generation cost amortizes over many executions and correctness can be ensured through extensive fuzz testing and manual inspection. For ad-hoc queries, GenDB can work with a traditional DBMS in a hybrid architecture: the DBMS handles one-off queries, while GenDB speeds up frequent SQL templates. We also discuss the current limitations of GenDB, such as high generation cost and the lack of correctness guarantees, to inform future extensions. papers.title: Future-Proof Data Systems
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Database systems are increasingly expected to support evolution in data workloads, representations, and hardware environments. Existing designs often respond through either specialization, which can deliver high performance but leads to narrow and brittle systems, or extensibility, which broadens functionality but can produce opaque extensions and growing system complexity. This paper summarizes a line of work that treats future-proofness as an abstraction-design problem: we identify boundaries across the data processing stack where concerns must evolve independently, and design interfaces that preserve enough structure across that boundary for optimization. We illustrate this at three levels of the stack. At the level of data structures, Sortledton unifies analytics, pattern matching, and transactional updates on a single graph representation. At the level of data formats, AnyBlox allows engines to read datasets that provide sandboxed self-decoding logic, reducing the need for bespoke readers. At the level of query processing, LingoDB and its declarative sub-operator layer recast query optimization as a sequence of extensible compiler passes, enabling cross-domain optimization and hardware-specific lowerings.

To retrieve complementary results, HeraDB maintains timestamp-based filters on both paths. This design mitigates PCIe bottlenecks by synchronizing lightweight timestamp logs rather than massive delta updates. Evaluation on HATtrick shows that HeraDB outperforms Colibri in maximum individual TP/AP throughput, achieving up to 11.1× higher TP and 5.9× higher AP with high data freshness and strong performance isolation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become pivotal for enhancing the capabilities of modern large models. Existing systems fail to address these two concerns in a unified manner. Techniques that tightly control data staleness often constrain effective data skewness mitigation, while aggressive data skewness mitigation tends to exacerbate data staleness. As a result, systems are forced to trade off convergence for performance, or vice versa. To address this, we propose StaleFlow, an RL post-training system that jointly tackles data staleness and skewness. First, to control staleness, StaleFlow introduces a global consistency protocol that tracks the full lifecycle of each trajectory and constrains staleness. Second, to mitigate skewness, StaleFlow re-designs the RL system architecture by constructing data servers for trajectories and parameters to achieve flexible rollout coordination. Subsequently, we develop a suite of staleness-aware, throughput-oriented strategies to enhance system performance. Evaluations show that StaleFlow achieves up to 1.42-2.68× (1.18-1.91× on average) higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems, without compromising convergence. Timely detection and remediation is paramount, but the constrained background resources on cloud may not keep pace. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Real-Time SPM in Oracle 26ai, a novel extension of SPM that performs foreground verification of new execution plans during user query execution. In this paper, we propose KLL-Polymer, the first per-key quantile sketch to achieve near-optimal space complexity. KLL-Polymer inherits the idea of hierarchical sampling from the KLL sketch, but aggregates items by key during the sampling process, thus enabling a single sketch to efficiently handle multiple keys, rather than maintaining separate KLL sketches for each key. We further introduce a deterministic-compaction variant of KLL-Polymer, which optimizes its performance by more effectively filtering infrequent keys at the top levels. papers.title: Tree+DAG: An Efficient Index for Resistance Distance Computation on Core-Periphery Graphs
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估，贴近真实场景，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Resistance distance computation is a fundamental problem in graph data management. To avoid the high latency of online evaluation, recent work builds offline indexes. Existing approaches, however, fall into two families with complementary weaknesses: loop-erased random-walk methods (e.g., LEIndex) are efficient on fast-mixing graphs but suffer high variance on sparse or tree-like topologies, whereas Cholesky-based methods (e.g., TreeIndex) perform well on small-treewidth graphs but are costly to construct for large, dense networks. In this work, we revisit the probabilistic structure of loop-erased random walks and reveal a previously unexplored connection between their distribution and the Cholesky decomposition of the inverse Laplacian. Building on this insight, we present Tree+DAG, an index that unifies deterministic matrix decomposition with loop-erased random walk sampling. We first apply a core–tree decomposition to split the graph into a tree-like periphery and a dense core. The periphery is isolated via TreeIndex—a compact hierarchical tree labelling that exploits the nonzero pattern of the Cholesky factors of the inverse Laplacian. In the core, random walks mix rapidly and thus erase few cycles; we propose CoreIndex, which stores the DAG encoding the erased cycle structure over the core. This design yields near-linear index size and build time, and low query latency in practice on graphs with a core–periphery structure. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets—including road, social, and web graphs with up to hundreds of millions of edges—show that Tree+DAG delivers at least an order-of-magnitude faster query performance than LEIndex. For example, on Twitter with 21,297,772 nodes and 265,025,545 edges, Tree+DAG attains absolute error 10^-2 with a modest index (3.1 GB, 1.5× the graph) built in 48 minutes, delivering over 3 orders of magnitude faster queries—8×10 -5 seconds vs. 7×10 -1 seconds for LEIndex.

Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. No single factor describes the slowdown between two environments: most of its variance lies between query templates, so a speed factor stops improving after a few queries. Large language models (LLMs) offer a different approach to index tuning, using knowledge they have learned from publicly available training data. However, the effectiveness of LLM-driven index tuning in comparison to today's index advisors, particularly on enterprise workloads, remains unclear. In this paper, we study the practical effectiveness of LLM-driven index tuning on Microsoft SQL Server using both industrial benchmarks and real-world enterprise customer workloads, and compare it with DTA. In this paper, we propose PRDCC, a prediction-driven framework for deterministic concurrency control, designed to mitigate abort-induced throughput collapse under high data contention. papers.title: Back to the Future: The Evolving Universal Relation Model

papers.abstract: Document backed analytics need databases that can be built as queries arrive. Schema first construction offers the opposite strength: once a database is built, it supports joins, aggregation, constraints, indexes, optimization, and transactions. We propose the Evolving Universal Relation Model (EUR), a query first model for document backed analytics. Users ask natural language queries as if the document corpus exposed one conceptual relation over application concepts. Internally, the DBMS turns each query into controlled database evolution: it updates the logical schema when new concepts are needed, extracts and integrates the facts required to answer the query, and decides what durable database state should remain for future queries. Thus, in EUR, a query is not only evaluated; it also helps construct the database. Document backed analytics becomes query first universal access plus workload-driven database schema and instance evolution.

In this paper, we study the efficient execution of the Maximum Connectivity-based γ-Quasi-Clique (MCQC) query, which seeks the γ-CQC with the largest number of vertices. The problem is NP-hard, and the non-hereditary nature of vertex connectivity invalidates many traditional pruning techniques, posing significant challenges for exact query processing. papers.title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems

papers.abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

papers.title: A Tree-Structured Two-Phase Commit Framework for OceanBase: Optimizing Scalability and Consistency
papers.importance_reason: 关注延迟
papers.abstract: Distributed transactional consistency over partitions is costly: classical two-phase commit (2PC) incurs high coordination and latency, and dynamic partition transfers complicate recovery. We introduce a tree-structured 2PC framework for OceanBase (OB) using single-machine log streams in three ways. First, we use log streams as coalesced 2PC participants: co-located partitions that would each be separate in a partition-centric design share one log-stream participant, so a transaction spanning N such partitions interacts with one participant in commit, cutting coordination by orders of magnitude (e.g., 99% for N = 100). Second, a coordinator-rooted DAG recursively builds commit trees; migration contexts as leaves avoid explicit participant-list updates and circular dependencies while ensuring linearizable commits under topology change. Third, prepare_unknown and trans_unknown states prevent violations when participants lose context; they signal uncertainty during retries, avoiding erroneous aborts from "lying" participants while isolating users from ambiguity. Experiments approach single-machine transaction performance with lower latency and bandwidth consumption, supporting modern distributed databases.

papers.title: CADENZA in Action: Breaking the Monolith with Intent-Dependent Plan Spaces for Semantic Queries
papers.importance_reason: 关注延迟
papers.abstract: Semantic query processing engines execute semantic operators, whose behavior is specified by natural-language intents, via model inference over multimodal data. Most existing optimizers optimize the operators at the granularity of monolithic implementations—such as LLMs and embedding models—forcing a trade-off between expensive model calls and cheaper alternatives that fail to capture intent-dependent semantics. We present CADENZA, a semantic operator optimizer that compiles an intent into decomposed steps, selects concrete physical implementations for each step, and tunes their parameters under user-specified quality-latency-cost preferences. In this demonstration, users interact with CADENZA through a web interface over multimodal databases, exploring how an intent is decomposed into alternative plans, how each plan is optimized, and how different preferences yield different winning plans.

papers.title: GraphAlg Playground: An Online Platform for Learning and Experimenting with the GraphAlg Language
papers.importance_reason: 有原型实现
papers.abstract: The GraphAlg language for graph algorithms enables native support for user-defined graph analytics workloads in databases. In this demonstration, we present a web-based playground for writing and executing GraphAlg programs in the web browser, including an interactive tutorial explaining its key concepts. The playground runs inside the user's web browser without any installation, and is freely available under a permissive license as a reusable library. We present two demonstration scenarios of the publicly available playground website, showing how new users can learn to program in GraphAlg using the tutorial, while expert users can use the playground to prototype and validate their algorithms.

papers.title: Guixu: Valuation-Driven Data Discovery for Autonomous AI Agents with On-Chain Attestation
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on external data to complete downstream tasks such as model training and decision support. However, existing data discovery systems remain largely retrieval-oriented: they surface candidate datasets from heterogeneous sources, but provide limited support for estimating task-specific utility, selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, or incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. This paper presents Guixu, a valuation-driven data discovery system for autonomous agents. Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline with proxy-label propagation and multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. Guixu integrates agentic payment protocol to enable budget-constrained data procurement workflows. Guixu leverages on-chain data market and attestation signals for verifiable data discovery. Our demonstration highlights how Guixu enables an agent to move beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval toward task- and budget-aware, trustworthy data discovery and procurement. Attendees can interactively explore the full workflow, from NL task specification and multi-source search to data valuation and verifiable transaction feedback.

papers.title: Hermes at Scale: Powering Distributed Queries with a Unified Memory Fabric
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: MySQL is a widely used database management system. However, it has clear deficits for analytical workloads. To improve analytical performance, we introduced Hermes as an accelerator for MySQL. Since many workloads easily fit a single node/machine, we originally developed Hermes for this case. However, Hermes on a single node has a major limitation: Storage space is limited to a single-node, even worse, to main memory of a single node. In this paper, we address this problem by making Hermes distributed. New nodes can be added that bring additional resources, i.e. memory and compute, to the cluster. Hermes' storage can automatically expand to the new nodes. Our design operates as logically "Shared Memory" via an abstraction layer (Memcom). We argue that modern interconnects make shared memory feasible without extreme performance penalties. To further minimize sending data over the network, we annotate larger data blocks with localities, which allows reader nodes to locate and read local data. In addition, we extended Hermes' query execution to multiple nodes as well. This is implemented via a new Planner that splits the query plan into tasks and defines how query execution is parallelized (MPP intra-query parallelism). Each task is separated via data sharing operators (Portals) that write intermediates to a shared memory pool (Memcom). We extended scans to pick up row groups (our granularity of data storage) based on their locality. Therefore, distributed scans will preferably read local data (thanks to our predefined localities) and only when there is no more local data to be read consider remote data. We experimentally show that our approach is not only competitive in terms of performance but outperforms well-known open-source systems by more than 11×. Compared to industrial-grade cloud systems, Hermes also outperforms by 1.5×.

papers.title: No Silver Bullet: Boosting GaussDB Performance on the 30TB TPC-H Workload

papers.abstract: GaussDB is Huawei's premier database system, designed for large-scale deployments and the most demanding workloads. It is a distributed shared-nothing system, capable of handling all types of workloads. This paper outlines a series of modifications to GaussDB aimed at improving its performance on large-scale and complex analytical workloads. After these changes, its performance on the TPC-H workload exceeded the best published result by 40% at 30 TB. The key enhancements to achieve this elite performance include adopting a pipeline execution model, a faster and more scalable inter-node data shuffle, exploiting a unified bus and unified remote memory access. We also expanded the support of cost-based Bloom filter placement and implemented several Bloom filter streaming strategies, enabling their use across nodes.

papers.title: ACTIVE: A Dynamic Pareto-Frontier-Based Unified Index for Dual-Vector Query
papers.importance_reason: 贴近真实场景，关注吞吐，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Existing approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) methods generally assume that each entity has a single vector. In many real-world applications, however, an entity is associated with more than one vector, and queries may jointly consider two attributes. With different queries assigning different weights to each attribute, Pareto-frontier-based indices provide an effective solution for dual-vector retrieval by connecting to approximate nearest neighbors under all possible query preferences. However, existing Pareto-frontier-based approaches suffer from substantial inefficiencies in both index construction and dynamic updates, limiting their practical applicability. To address these issues, we propose ACTIVE, a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance under varying query preferences. It employs angle-constrained active-range computation and connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategies to accelerate node insertion and deletion, respectively. Extensive experiments show that, at comparable (or slightly below) search accuracy, ACTIVE improves insertion throughput by $1.20$--$1.43\times$ over DEG, and deletion throughput by $1.64$--$2.06\times$ over neighbor-reconnection-based repair and by $22.64$--$39.51\times$ over reinsertion-based repair.

papers.title: Revision-Bound Evidence Cuts: Authenticated Queries and Contextual Witness Capacity

papers.abstract: Authentic records can support unauthorized narratives when their qualifications, query scope, or counterevidence are silently dropped. We present revision-bound evidence cuts, a framework for authenticating both supporting and opposing inference obligations across changing source versions. Signed complete-update frontiers permit transport of unaffected certificates, alternative-cut recovery, and an exact certified-reuse radius given by a frontier-hypergraph transversal number. Their source obligations induce an integral model of context-bound authorization. To secure database-derived claims, we introduce an authenticated relational query contract that binds original source records, complete selected bags, counting units, parameters, and aggregates independently of execution strategy. A full-source verifier checks 16,824 Chogha Mish records across SQLite scans, indexes, and materialized views; three valid strategies agree and eight contract/view mutations are rejected. A separate 340-row NISP cohort shows that changing the admitted weighting rule can reverse a comparison while preserving every source record. A frozen English text-to-frame compiler produces qualified evidence receipts, with linguistic accuracy evaluated separately from cryptographic integrity. We also separate logical-source from transport commitments so lossless re-encoding need not invalidate unchanged scientific evidence. The SCENE prototype evaluates signed revisions, authenticated queries, scoped disclosures, and adversarial mutations at scales reaching one million source records. These guarantees rely on declared policies and independently pinned trust roots; they authenticate specified computations and obligations, not historical truth, complete counterevidence, or institutional endorsement.

papers.title: Taming Multi-Dimensional Skew in Sparse Matrix Multiplication with Contention-Aware Scheduling [Technical Report]
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，有实验评估，贴近真实场景
papers.abstract: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) is a key kernel in graph analytics, relational queries, and machine learning. Yet, its performance remains a significant challenge, due to the inherent sparsity and, more critically, the prevalent skew patterns often found in real-world workloads. This paper investigates this problem and demonstrates that an unbalanced workload distribution is the main culprit, harming performance through two co-existing root causes: first, multi-dimensional skew, where imbalance across computation cost, output density, and data locality cannot be captured by any single balancing metric; and second, cache contention, where dense substructures induce severe on-chip interference. To that end, we propose adaptive morsel scheduling (AMS), a dynamic scheduling framework that decouples skew dimensions via fixed-result-size morsels and integrates contention-aware load balancing (CALB) and data-conscious simultaneous multithreading activator (SMTact) to alleviate cache-level contention, alongside a hybrid accumulation mechanism (HYB) that adaptively selects the best accumulator per morsel. Evaluations across matrix squaring, relational queries, graph analytics, and other sparse matrix kernels show that AMS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on skewed workloads while maintaining comparable performance on non-skewed ones. These gains, along with improved bandwidth utilization, remain valid across a wide range of workloads and hardware systems.

papers.title: Supervised and LLM-Augmented Cardinality Estimation for Similarity Queries on Knowledge Graphs

papers.abstract: Over the past decades, query cardinality estimation on relational databases has been proven crucial, enabling the result size estimation of all sub-plans of each query. This allowed query optimizers to design efficient query plans, towards minimizing the query response time. Lately, knowledge graphs are being preferred over traditional databases in various applications, due to their ability to represent complex relationships and semantic meaning in a domain-specific context. In this work, we present a novel approach for supervised similarity-aware cardinality estimation on knowledge graphs that incorporates similarities into the model training process, thus treating them as first-class citizens. To this end, we present SCE-KG, a model that employs a novel encoding scheme for cardinality estimation, named SGsplit. We further extend our approach by leveraging a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate training queries that resemble realistic user workloads, and show that combining LLM-generated and random walk samples consistently improves estimation accuracy on test workloads generated by two independent LLMs. Our experimental evaluation reveals that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques in terms of prediction error, achieving 40x and 37x improvement for star and chain queries, respectively (95th percentile), whereas its online overhead accounts for less than 0.05% of the average query execution time and less than 1% of the average query planning time, showing a sub-millisecond latency in all cases.

papers.abstract: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

papers.title: Navigating Runtime Dynamism in Semantic Query Serving
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，关注延迟，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.

papers.title: G-CasDec: General Cascaded Decompression on GPUs
papers.importance_reason: 涉及压缩
papers.abstract: GPU-accelerated analytical query processing is often limited by both GPU device memory capacity and host-to-device data transfer time. Modern data compression techniques, such as cascaded lightweight compression, can mitigate these issues. However, existing designs all exhibit critical tradeoffs on compression ratios, decompression speed, and extensibility. They either apply aggressive compression without addressing execution irregularity, or maintain strictly aligned data layouts that sacrifice compressibility. Also, none of them provides an extensible way to easily add new schemes. To address these issues, we present G-CasDec, an optimized framework to enable efficient decompression on GPUs for general cascaded compression schemes. G-CasDec incorporates several key techniques, including aligned batching for aggressive compression of variable-length data yet with efficient decompression, shared memory reuse and register-level fusion to improve resource utilization, and a set of bytecode instructions to orchestrate a generic decompression flow. G-CasDec outperforms state-of-the-art designs with 2.8× higher compression ratios and 2.0× faster decompression, and is also extensible to arbitrary cascade schemes.

papers.title: Recovering Business Rules as Cascade Lookups for Enterprise Field Prediction

papers.abstract: Enterprise sales-order systems rely on manually maintained configuration rules to determine fields such as payment terms, shipping points, and sales ownership. We introduce a knowledge-graph-guided workflow in which an LLM agent proposes candidate business keys, meaning column combinations such as customer and document type, validates them through SQL profiling, and compiles the resulting evidence into deterministic cascade lookups. The LLM is used only during offline rule discovery. At inference time, prediction is a transparent key lookup with no model-serving requirement. Experiments on enterprise sales-order prediction and public relational benchmarks show that cascades are most effective when fields follow stable business rules, while learned graph models remain preferable when prediction depends on temporal or neighborhood patterns. Drift analysis further turns residual errors into diagnostics for configuration maintenance. Code and data: https://github.com/Fireblossom/CascadER.

papers.title: When the Application Layer Is Disposable: Putting Integrity Constraints Back in the Database
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，涉及基数估计
papers.abstract: Integrity constraints have been central to the relational model since its inception. However, beyond keys, single-row CHECKs, and referential integrity, most constraints are enforced by application layers today. SQL ASSERTIONs, standardized in SQL-92, remain poorly supported by major RDBMSs. This has become increasingly unacceptable due to two developments. First, LLM-driven applications and agents increasingly issue queries and updates directly against databases, bypassing application layers where invariants reside. Such code may be generated on demand and discarded afterwards, making the database the only durable component that can encode and enforce these invariants. Second, natural constraints in higher-level conceptual models, such as E/R and property graphs, become fragmented across relations under mappings chosen for performance. The resulting multi-relation constraints lack direct database support, and only some can be efficiently enforced using existing mechanisms such as triggers. These developments motivate an overhaul of how constraints are defined, mined, managed, and enforced in data management systems. As a first concrete step, we introduce constraint indexes, which represent constraints spanning multiple relations as transactional access paths, and implement a proof of concept as a PostgreSQL extension. Constraint indexes enforce constraints arising from distributed inheritance hierarchies, folded relationships, and folded weak entities, as well as cardinality bounds and functional dependencies, at low overhead relative to no enforcement. Across these workloads, they outperform the better of the correctness-preserving baselines by up to 2.41 times. We also show that LLM-driven writers frequently violate unenforced constraints and behave erratically when provided with a list of constraints to enforce. We close by discussing a few research challenges raised by this agenda.

papers.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed

papers.abstract: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.

papers.title: Fidelity Synopses: Pre-Execution Plan Selection for Approximate Vector Search
papers.importance_reason: 带基准测试，涉及基数估计
papers.abstract: Vector search has become a database operator with many physical implementations: different index families, build-time and search-time parameters, and compressed or disk-resident variants. Each trades cost against fidelity, the fraction of a query's exact top-k nearest neighbors that a configuration returns. Deployments nevertheless choose one configuration offline and use it for every query, so they are sized for their hardest queries and overpay for the rest. On a 5.8M-item LAION benchmark with four embedding models, running each query on the cheapest configuration that suffices for it would roughly halve the cost in a typical setting. Exploiting this requires predicting each configuration's fidelity before running it, which is hard because fidelity is defined by the very exact search that approximate indexes avoid. Relational optimizers solve the analogous problem for cardinality with offline synopses; we propose one for vector search. A fidelity synopsis divides the embedding space into cells around a set of landmarks and records, for every cell and configuration, how often that configuration met a fidelity target on a sample of queries. At query time, one nearest-landmark lookup yields a calibrated estimate for every configuration, and an optimizer chooses configurations so that the workload misses the target no more often than its requirement allows. We test the two premises the synopsis relies on, that fidelity varies smoothly across the embedding space and that its loss is specific to each configuration. Held to the same requirement a static deployment is built to meet, synopsis-guided selection lowers cost in all 16 combinations of model and query direction, to a median of 0.72x the static deployment, with a batched lookup of 21-32 microseconds per query. The saving persists against the best static choice among the same indexes, and within a single index at no extra memory.

papers.title: Modular and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search with Vectorium and kANNolo

papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) search over neural embeddings powers modern retrieval systems such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Embeddings come in three representations (dense, sparse and multi-vector), and efficient search combines an index structure, a similarity function and a quantization scheme. Existing libraries fix one combination, hard-code each one separately, or factor only one side of the problem, and none covers all three representations. We present Vectorium and kANNolo, two open-source Rust libraries that split this design space into a data-management layer and an indexing layer. Vectorium abstracts the vector, the distance function, the quantizer and the dataset independently, and provides 11 encoders, from 32-bit floats to sub-bit codes. On top of it, kANNolo implements Hierarchical Navigable Small-World (HNSW) graph and Inverted Vector File (IVF) indexes that are generic over representation, encoder and metric, and a two-stage index that composes any first-stage index with any rescoring dataset. Since every combination is specialized at compile time, this modularity adds no run-time overhead, and the resulting indexes reach state-of-the-art performance: our Product Quantization matches Faiss in accuracy at competitive speed, our RaBitQ and HNSW match or outperform their reference implementations, and our IVF outperforms Faiss. Against six dense and five sparse systems on seven public collections, our indexes give the best memory-throughput trade-off on dense data in 9 of 12 collection-accuracy pairs and perform well on out-of-distribution queries. On sparse data, the systems built on Vectorium lead on all three collections, with Seismic and SeismicWave the fastest and kANNolo's indexes the most compact.

These approaches inadequately capture boundary structure and local spatial context, causing topology-sensitive relationships near geometry boundaries to be underrepresented in the learned embedding space. Consequently, accurately modeling complex spatial interactions remains a significant challenge for downstream spatial reasoning tasks. To fill the gap, we introduce SpatialVec, a boundary-aware spatial representation learning framework that adaptively samples geometry boundaries and their surrounding regions, capturing fine-grained geometric structures critical for topology-aware spatial reasoning. A transformer-based encoder-decoder trained through geometry reconstruction produces compact, geometry-aware, and unified representations for points, polylines, and polygons. Empirical evaluation on two real-world datasets shows that SpatialVec substantially improves the preservation of challenging topological relationships involving polygonal interactions and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines significantly on downstream prediction and classification tasks.

papers.title: Tessera: Fast Join-Aggregates over Skewed Sparse Relations in Database Engines

papers.abstract: Join-aggregate queries count or sum matching rows for each pair of values, often over skewed sparse relations in which a few values are frequent and most pairs of values never co-occur. Conventional execution plans materialize billions of intermediate join rows, taking minutes to tens of minutes per query. Recent matrix-based solutions reformulate these queries as matrix multiplication to reduce or avoid this materialization. However, they remain slow because they either store result cells for non-matching pairs or still materialize intermediate join rows for infrequent values. We present Tessera, a skew-aware join-aggregate operator for database engines that avoids both sources of overhead. Specifically, Tessera computes a sparse matrix product directly over the engine's rows, emits only nonzero cells as result rows, and prunes values that cannot meet the query's threshold before multiplication begins. It also offloads the dense block formed by pairs of the most frequent values to a CPU matrix accelerator when that block is dense enough. Experimental results show that Tessera is faster than the fastest existing system by 2.8x to 18.8x. In addition, Tessera outperforms DuckDB's execution plans by up to 1,802x.

papers.abstract: Data access is often limited by privacy or proprietary restrictions, motivating relational database synthesis, which synthesizes realistic contents across related tables. In this paper, we propose REMIX, a unified framework for realistic relational database synthesis with mixed-type attributes. REMIX integrates a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM) through two key phases: Graph-to-Prompt Tuning and Collaborative SLM-LLM Decoding. To capture attribute dependencies within and across tables, Graph-to-Prompt Tuning represents the database as an attributed heterogeneous graph. We project mixed-type record embeddings and aggregated relational context into soft prompts that serve as continuous vectors for an SLM. We jointly optimize the graph-to-prompt mapping and SLM through autoregressive attribute reconstruction. Furthermore, to reduce semantic inconsistencies, Collaborative SLM-LLM Decoding combines SLM-based record generation with repair programs induced by an LLM. The LLM discovers semantic dependencies, iteratively refines them through independent validation with a statistical bound on the overall probability of false acceptance, and translates validated dependencies into tested programs that repair generated values. Extensive experiments on seven real-world relational databases demonstrate the effectiveness of REMIX in generating high-fidelity data with improved semantic consistency and downstream utility.

papers.title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures

papers.abstract: A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible. We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time. We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

papers.abstract: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose. Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.

papers.title: SPARQLcirc: Probabilistic Query Evaluation with Provenance Circuits
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) computes the probability of every answer of a query over a tuple-independent probabilistic knowledge graph. We study exact PQE for SPARQL over graphs accessed through SPARQL 1.1 endpoints. Shared triples among the derivations of an answer make exact PQE #P-hard in general. Knowledge compilation of the Boolean provenance of every answer yields exact probabilities, and the provenance formulas of different answers can share subformulas. We propose SPARQLcirc, which rewrites a SPARQL query into CONSTRUCT queries that name every gate by its content, so that the results of independent queries form one Boolean provenance circuit for all answers. The rewriting covers joins, unions, projection, filters, OPTIONAL, difference, and transitive closures. SPARQLcirc compiles the circuit and computes the exact probability of every answer by weighted model counting. For the evaluation, we draw random probabilities for the triples of WatDiv and gMark and the statements of Wikidata and evaluate the CONSTRUCT queries on GraphDB, Fuseki, and Oxigraph. The ratio of the end-to-end time of PQE with SPARQLcirc to that of PQE by compiling the provenance expressions of the SPARQL provenance rewriting NPCS decreases with the number of derivations.

papers.title: A Multimodal Type 2 Diabetes Registry on DHIS2: A Design and Feasibility Study with the AI-READI Dataset
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Care for type 2 diabetes increasingly draws on continuous glucose monitors, wearable devices, home sensors, clinical records and retinal images, yet few open platforms have been shown to hold all of these for the same person. We asked three questions of DHIS2, the open-source health information system that ministries of health in about 80 countries run nationally: whether an unmodified Tracker program can represent these modalities together (RQ1), which design choices its row-per-event data model forces for dense sensor streams (RQ2), and what a bulk loader must do to load such data correctly (RQ3). We designed a registry of 27 program stages and 445 data elements, loaded the AI-READI dataset of 2,280 participants into it, and verified the result field by field against the source files. The program held every loaded modality in 8.09 million events. Dense streams were stored as hourly summaries aligned across modalities; electrocardiograms, diagnoses and 118,480 retinal images were stored as one event per record. The event model ruled out storing raw readings, and hourly summaries reduced the wearable and glucose volume about 26-fold. An audit of the loader found defects that shared one pattern: a failure that looked like success. We state five lessons for DHIS2 Tracker clients that address this pattern. Verification of all 64.9 million stored values found four defects, all missing, duplicated or artifactual records rather than wrong values, and none after their repair; an independent recomputation of the glucose summaries agreed on all 464,210 values compared. The paper offers implementation guidance for DHIS2 implementers and for users of AI-READI; it does not evaluate clinical use. Analytics at this scale, use by clinicians and live device feeds remain to be shown.

papers.title: CypherGuard: Database-Grounded Correction for Reliable Text-to-Cypher
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Text-to-Cypher translates natural-language questions into Cypher queries over property graphs. Graph database systems increasingly adopt this translation as a native query interface. Large language models generate fluent Cypher but stay unreliable. On Cypher-Bench a small model answers only 31.4% of questions correctly, and even a strong model plateaus at 71.76%. The dominant failure modes are structural rather than linguistic. For example, a generated query may parse correctly and follow the schema, yet still return zero rows because it traverses a relationship against the stored graph direction. To address this issue, we present CypherGuard, a training-free framework that detects and corrects these structural faults. Our approach uses two core components: a graph-native error taxonomy to guide repair, and a mined rule library to guide query generation. At inference time, CypherGuard first rewrites schema-detectable faults, then re-executes each draft and repairs it only when the query errors or returns nothing. On CypherBench test questions, across seven graphs, CypherGuard reaches 88.50% overall execution accuracy, +25.08% over the same-backbone zero-shot floor, surpassing an RL-fine-tuned 7B specialist and the strongest training-based system that we compare against.

papers.title: Graphs Have Structure: Declarative Manifolds, 3D Z-Order Monoid Roll-ups, and Zero-Simulation Visual Analytics in a Graph DBMS
papers.importance_reason: 贴近真实场景
papers.abstract: Every real-world graph is embedded in an ambient structural manifold: proteins fold in Euclidean space ($R^3$), telecom networks sit on a planetary surface ($S^2 \times R$), and ontologies and calendars form discrete subsumption posets ($(V, \sqsubseteq)$). Yet property graph databases treat node coordinates as opaque payload scalars, leave spatial proximity edges unindexed, and force visualizers into $O(V^2)$ client-side force-directed simulations that destroy true geometry and truncate hierarchy roll-ups. We elevate ambient manifold structure to a first-class primitive in Samyama Graph. First, we introduce a declarative and auto-detected structural convention contract (samyama.structure/1) persisted in .sgsnap headers that binds node labels to Euclidean 3D, Geo-Spherical, Causal Spacetime, or Poset Hierarchy manifolds. Second, we show that both discrete posets (via Order-Embedded Hierarchy $[tin, tout]$ DFS intervals) and continuous 3D manifolds (via a 63-bit 3D Morton Z-order Structural-Geometric Index, SGI) reduce regional aggregation to 1D rank-interval monoid folds answered directly from index-resident Fenwick trees (SUM, COUNT) and Segment Trees (MIN, MAX). At $100,000$ 3D nodes, SGI builds in $28.14$ ms and answers Morton-interval SUM and MAX roll-ups in $0.048\,μ$s and $0.104\,μ$s---$8,345.1\times$ and $3,824.4\times$ faster than property scans. Third, we introduce 3D voxel-hashed virtual contact edges weighted by Topological--Geometric Stress $σ(u,v) = d_{graph}(u,v) / d_{manifold}(u,v)$ to isolate long-range tertiary folds, plus manifold-guided $A^*$ shortest-path search that cuts explored states by up to $3.80\times$ over Dijkstra. Fourth, we replace client layout simulation with server-computed 3D Cone-Tree/Ribbon coordinates and a non-WebGL 2.5D Isometric projection with painter's-order depth sorting and sub-millisecond Level-of-Detail (LoD) macro-cuts.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic queries over unstructured data, but invoking an LLM on every row is prohibitively expensive. Proxy-based execution can reduce this ple with the LLM and training a lightweight proxyto label the remaining rows. Nevertheless, in practical scenarios where semantic queries are highly selective, it remainschallenging to identify representative samples foLM budget and to achieve accurate predictions overthe remaining data using the proxy. We present PROBE, a learned proxy-based execution framework for highly selective multimodal semantic queries. PROBE uses selectivity-adaptive sampling to discover rare polightweight proxy on the acquired labels. It thenrefines proxy predictions through residual correction and homogeneity smoothing over a similarity graph. To address sampling bias, PROBE jointly calibrates refined scores usiarate calibration sample, then selectively routescandidates to the LLM by optimizing the tradeoff between estimated F1 and evaluation cost. On queries from SemBench and LRO-Bench with positive rates as low as 2.17x10^-5 budget yields a geometric-mean F1 of 0.762,compared with 0.797 for exhaustive LLM evaluation, at a geometric-mean speedup of 4.87x and a maximum speedup of 9.3x.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Lakehouse: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Managing Enterprise Knowledge Graphs at Scale
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse through metadata, indexes, and caching. Enterprise knowledge graphs (KGs) offer an alternative approach to such integration for the purposes of data analysis, but handling them at scale must address the Three Vs of big data: volume, velocity, and variety. Contextualized KGs (CKGs) meet part of that challenge by enriching facts with contextual information, yet many applications require only a context-specific subset of that knowledge. We propose the Knowledge Graph Lakehouse (KG Lakehouse), a cloud-native microservice architecture that adapts the data lakehouse paradigm for management of CKGs at scale. The KG Lakehouse indexes incoming source documents along configurable context dimensions and stores these documents in a data lake, from which application-specific CKGs are constructed on demand instead of maintaining a single, monolithic KG. We realize the proposed architecture as a proof of concept, with independently deployable services built from established cloud technology; context dimensions and format-specific document handling enter as configuration, leaving the architecture independent of the application domain. We evaluate the implemented system in experiments on a distributed cluster deployment.

papers.title: Optimizing Geo-replicated Deterministic Databases
papers.importance_reason: 关注吞吐
papers.abstract: In transactional databases, achieving active-active replication among geo-distributed replicas is challenging due to the high coordination cost in ensuring the serializability of concurrent cross-node transactions. Deterministic concurrency control (DCC) has emerged as a promising alternative: it establishes a global order for a batch of transactions before execution and thereby amortizes this coordination cost across the batch. To better understand the performance characteristics of DCC, we conduct a theoretical analysis of traditional two-phase locking and optimistic concurrency control to account for geo-replication and introduce a model for DCC. We compare the three paradigms and identify the conditions under which DCC is advantageous. Guided by the insights from this analysis, we then present Quirinus, a DCC-based geo-replicated database that optimizes transaction execution through speculative execution, transaction reordering, integration of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), and fast-path commit. Even without these optimizations, Quirinus achieves up to 6.2x the TPC-C throughput of Tiga under our configuration.

papers.title: Order-Dependent Complexity of Enumeration and Direct Access for Conjunctive Queries on Dynamic Data
papers.importance_reason: 涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: This note studies the fine-grained complexity of ranked enumeration and ranked direct access of conjunctive query answers over a dynamic database. We focus on lexicographically sorted answers, defined by an ordering on the query's free variables. From the literature, when no particular order is required, we know that when the query is self-join-free and q-hierarchical, we can build a data structure for enumeration (resp. direct access) with linear (resp. linearithmic) preprocessing and constant (resp. logarithmic) update time in the size of the database. For enumeration (resp. direct access), this data structure yields an algorithm that enumerates all query answers (resp. that returns the $k$-th query answer) with constant delay (resp. logarithmic access time). Our goal is to extend these results to ranked enumeration and ranked direct access, with the ranking function defined by a lexicographic order. We define a property on the order over the variables of $Q$, which we call being hierarchy-consistent. Given a user-specified query and hierarchy-consistent order, we first propose, for ranked enumeration under updates, an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that enumerates all the query answers according to the user-specified order with constant delay. Moreover, for ranked direct access under updates, we propose an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that returns the $k$-th tuple according to the user-specified order with logarithmic access time. In contrast, given a user-specified query and non-hierarchy-consistent order, we show a lower bound for ranked direct access under updates.
